Great spotted woodpecker, treecreeper and ring-necked parakeet breed, and bats hunt above the ponds.

en.location: 📍 Overveen, between Bloemendaal and Zandvoort · Dune wood · Medium-sized
en.description: Middenduin lies on the inner dune edge near Overveen and bears the traces of a striking piece of agricultural history: the dune fields. In the nineteenth century, parcels in the dune valleys were dug out to just above the groundwater, so that crops could reach moisture even in dry summers. On those artificially lowered fields, potatoes and vegetables were grown for Haarlem and Amsterdam. Such sand-stripped flats are now botanically valuable: the digging brought lime-rich sand to the surface, and it is precisely there that rare dune plants grow. Orchids, grass-of-Parnassus and dune pansy occur, and nightingale and woodlark breed.

en.description: The Brouwerskolkpark owes its name to the breweries that once stood here. At the dune foot, dune water surfaces: rainwater filtered through tens of metres of lime-rich sand, emerging crystal clear and free of germs. In an age when city water was dangerously polluted, that dune water was worth its weight in gold — Haarlem brewers accordingly settled here, and Haarlem beer owed its fame partly to this source. Later the same principle was applied on an industrial scale when Amsterdam began drawing its drinking water from the dunes in 1853. The park now has old trees, ponds and brooks, with kingfisher, nuthatch and bats.

nl.description: Het Kraansvlak is beroemd geworden als het eerste gebied van West-Europa waar sinds 2007 weer wisenten — Europese bizons — vrij rondlopen. De achterliggende gedachte is ecologisch: het duin groeide dicht met struweel en gras doordat konijnen door ziektes waren gedecimeerd en grote grazers al eeuwen ontbraken. en.description: The Kraansvlak became famous as the first area in Western Europe where wisents — European bison — have roamed free again since 2007. The reasoning is ecological: the dunes had grown over with scrub and grass because rabbits had been decimated by disease and large grazers had been absent for centuries. Wisents do what no mowing machine can: they rub against bushes, take sand baths and strip bark from trees, creating open sandy patches and varied structure. The experiment has been followed internationally. On the resulting open patches, sand lizard, wheatear, Niobe fritillary and rare dune flora benefit.

en.location: 📍 Overveen, inner dune edge · Country estate · Medium-sized
en.description: Elswout is one of the oldest and largest estates on the inner dune edge, laid out from 1634 by the Amsterdam merchant Carel Gaeff. The layout shows how much money and power circulated in the Golden Age: the dune terrain was literally dug away and remade — dune tops removed, valleys deepened, ponds and watercourses created with water that welled from the dunes of its own accord. Sand released was shipped to Amsterdam to raise the foundations of the canal ring. The works thus paid for themselves. Now centuries-old beeches and oaks stand here, with tawny owl, nuthatch, stock dove, bats and a rich stinzen flora.

en.description: Koningshof is a small country estate at the dune foot near Overveen, part of the almost continuous series of estates stretching from Haarlem to Zandvoort. That concentration is no accident: the inner dune edge offered everything a seventeenth-century merchant sought — high dry ground that did not flood, clean dune water, shelter from the sea wind, and a location a few hours’ sail from Amsterdam. The result is one of the densest concentrations of historic country estates in Europe. At Koningshof stand old trees with cavities and dead wood, benefiting nuthatch, great spotted woodpecker, tawny owl and bats; in spring stinzen flora blooms.

en.location: 📍 Between Zandvoort and Haarlem · Dune routes · Long
en.description: The Visserspad (Fishermen’s Path) is one of the oldest routes in Kennemerland: for centuries Zandvoort fishwives walked it with baskets of fresh fish on their heads to the market in Haarlem. That journey of over ten kilometres through loose dune sand was often made in the dark, for the fish had to be on the market by morning. Only with the railway in 1881 did the trade vanish. The Duinpieperpad is named after the tawny pipit, a bird that bred in these dunes into the 1980s but has since disappeared as a Dutch breeding bird — a name that thus marks a loss. Along both paths lie grey dunes, scrub and slacks with nightingale, wheatear and dune flora.

en.description: The Mr. H. Enschedépark in Heemstede is named after the Enschedé family, the Haarlem printing dynasty that from the eighteenth century produced, among other things, Dutch banknotes and postage stamps. Like many wealthy families they bought a country estate on the inner dune edge; when the park passed to the municipality in the twentieth century, the name was kept. The layout is in landscape style, with winding ponds and groups of old trees. The combination of water, old trees and shelter makes the park surprisingly rich: kingfisher, nuthatch, great spotted woodpecker and ring-necked parakeet breed, and bats hunt above the ponds.

en.location: 📍 Bloemendaal, inner dune edge · Country estate · Small
en.description: Naaldenveld is an estate on the inner dune edge near Bloemendaal, with strikingly much conifer woodland — hence the name (naald = needle). Those conifers were a nineteenth-century choice: on the poor, dry dune sands broadleaves grew slowly, whereas Scots pine and Austrian pine thrived and moreover yielded timber quickly. Austrian pine was even brought specially from Austria because it tolerates sea wind and salt where other species die off. So arose the dark pine woods found throughout the dune region. They are ecologically poorer than broadleaf wood, but do provide nest sites for goshawk, sparrowhawk and long-eared owl, and unusual fungi grow there.

en.location: 📍 Between Zandvoort, Vogelenzang and Noordwijk · Dune area · Very large
en.description: The Amsterdam Water Supply Dunes cover over 3400 hectares and owe their existence to a cholera epidemic. After Amsterdam was repeatedly struck by cholera in the nineteenth century through polluted canal water, a pipeline was built in 1853 bringing clean dune water to the city — the first modern drinking-water system in the Netherlands. To protect that source the city bought the entire dune area, and it is precisely that protection which made it one of the richest reserves in the country. Since 1957 river water has been infiltrated into the dunes, creating broad lagoons and humid slacks. Fallow deer, foxes, roe deer and more than a thousand plant species live here.

nl.description: Leyduin, Vinkenduin en Oud Woestduin vormen samen een aaneengesloten landgoedzone op de binnenduinrand. De naam Vinkenduin verwijst naar de vinkenbanen die hier lagen: installaties waarmee trekvogels massaal werden gevangen. In het najaar trekken langs de kust miljoenen vinken, en met lokvogels, netten en lokfluitjes ving men er duizenden tegelijk — voor de pot, als kooivogel en voor de handel. The name Vinkenduin (finch dune) refers to the finch-catching grounds that lay here: installations with which migrating birds were caught en masse. In autumn millions of finches pass along the coast, and with decoys, nets and whistles thousands were caught at a time — for the pot, as cage birds and for trade. It was a regular industry until bird protection ended it in the early twentieth century. The estates are now well wooded, with stinzen flora, old beeches and seepage brooks; tawny owl, nuthatch, kingfisher breed and bats live here.

tags: Duck decoy · historic trapping installation in the polder
en.location: 📍 Haarlemmermeer, near Vijfhuizen · Duck decoy · Very small
en.description: A duck decoy is among the most ingenious trapping installations ever developed in the Netherlands. Around a pond lie curved, progressively narrowing pipes, spanned with netting and screened by reed fences. The decoyman uses a kooikerhondje, a small dog that runs up and down along the screens; wild ducks are so curious about this little predator that they swim after it into the pipe, from which they cannot return. Tame call ducks lure their fellows in. Around a decoy the ancient right of enclosure applies: within a radius of hundreds of metres no disturbance is permitted — which has made decoys refuges for centuries.

en.location: 📍 Haarlemmermeer, near Zwanenburg · Polder wood · Medium-sized
en.description: The Meerbos lies in the Haarlemmermeer polder, a remarkable place in landscape terms: until 1852 a large inland lake lay here that storms made eat away at its shores so fiercely that it threatened Amsterdam and Leiden. The lake was pumped dry with three steam engines — at the time a technical feat of world class. The exposed floor lies five metres below sea level and consists of heavy, wet marine clay. Planting woodland on such ground is difficult: roots tolerate wet clay poorly. The Meerbos therefore consists largely of poplar, ash and willow. Goshawk, great spotted woodpecker and kingfisher breed.

It is now mature enough for hole-nesters and raptors: goshawk, great spotted woodpecker, nuthatch, and the pools attract kingfisher, grebes and dragonflies.

en.description: Eikenrode is a small estate in Heemstede with a name made of two old landscape words. Rode or rade means cleared land — a place where woodland was felled to make arable. It recurs in hundreds of Dutch place names (Roden, Rijsbergen, Nieuwerode) and dates from the great medieval clearance wave between the tenth and thirteenth centuries, when population grew and woodland everywhere was converted to farmland. That an oak wood was once cleared here and trees were later planted again is a pleasing full circle. The park now has old trees, a pond and stinzen flora, with nuthatch, woodpecker and bats.

Nuthatch, woodpecker and ring-necked parakeet breed.

en.description: The Bennebroekbos belongs to the series of estate woods clothing the inner dune edge between Haarlem and Hillegom. What makes these woods ecologically special is their stinzen flora: bulbs and spring plants such as snowdrop, wild tulip, hollowroot and bluebell, deliberately planted here centuries ago by the estate owners. The word stinze comes from Frisian and means stone house; the flora was named after those noble residences. Many species are not originally native but come from central and southern Europe, and they have made themselves thoroughly at home in the lime-rich, sheltered dune soil. Tawny owl, nuthatch and great spotted woodpecker breed.
